name: Bimax / double jaw surgery
lead: Bimaxillary ("bimax") surgery, also called double jaw surgery, repositions the upper and lower jaws in one operation. It typically combines a Le Fort I osteotomy of the maxilla with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) of the mandible, and a chin procedure may be added.[1] Because both jaws move, the surgeon can change the bite, the length and projection of the lower face, the position of the chin and the support under the nose and lips together.

It is an established orthognathic procedure used for malocclusion, jaw asymmetry, receding or protruding jaws and obstructive sleep apnea, normally after a period of orthodontic preparation.[1] The combined technique is associated with the Austrian surgeon Hugo Obwegeser, who published a paper on simultaneous maxillary and mandibular surgery around 1969 to 1970.[19] In looksmaxxing communities the word has become shorthand for the most comprehensive jaw surgery, and members discuss it as a way to reshape facial proportions, with threads weighing it against fillers and implants, braces-only treatment, multi-segment versions and surgery with maxillary skeletal expansion.[4][5][6][7] Wikipedia lists jaw surgery among the cosmetic surgeries that hardmaxxers pursue and says maxillofacial surgery is frequently proposed and discussed among looksmaxxers.[18]

Published research focuses on bite, airway and quality-of-life outcomes. A 2025 systematic review of 22 cohort studies (1,482 participants) examined what influences quality of life after orthognathic surgery,[8] and a 2022 meta-analysis of 20 studies on facial attractiveness reported that orthodontics plus orthognathic surgery added a further improvement of about 5.5 percent over orthodontics alone, which the authors described as clinically weak.[23] Reviews describe functional and aesthetic benefits alongside the risks of a major operation.[1][8]

chain: Upper and lower jaws are cut and moved to planned positions
Bite, jaw projection, chin position and facial proportions change
A different facial profile and lower-face shape
angle.text: Moving both jaws changes the bone framework that the soft tissue of the lower face rests on. Surgeons plan the movements with imaging software that can predict the post-operative face, and members of looksmaxxing communities seek it for profile, recession, underbite or asymmetry changes that other methods do not alter [1].

paras: The Le Fort I osteotomy cuts the maxilla horizontally so the upper jaw can be moved forward, back, up or down and fixed with plates and screws.[1] Its name echoes the French surgeon Rene Le Fort, who in the early 1900s described patterns of midface fracture; Wikipedia describes the Le Fort I fracture as a horizontal break through the maxilla between the hard palate and the orbits.[20] Obwegeser is credited with developing the modern Le Fort I osteotomy that fully mobilises the maxilla through pterygomaxillary disjunction.[19] Maxillary impaction is described as riskier than some other movements.[1]

The BSSO splits the mandible lengthwise on each side so the lower jaw can slide forward or back; Wikipedia says it was developed by Hugo Obwegeser and that titanium plates and screws now usually hold it, rather than prolonged jaw wiring.[1] A chin procedure (genioplasty) may be added to advance, set back or reshape the chin; Wikipedia describes sliding genioplasty as moving a horseshoe-shaped piece of the lower jaw and notes that orthognathic surgery is used when a small chin coexists with a significant overbite, since cosmetic chin procedures alone do not correct the bite.[1][22]

A team of oral and maxillofacial surgeons and orthodontists plans the case with radiographs, photographs and software that predicts the post-operative facial shape; airway protection is a key planning concern, and a psychological assessment is occasionally required.[1] A 2026 preprint review of 16 studies of virtual planning in bimaxillary surgery reported mean discrepancies between plan and outcome within 2 mm and 2 degrees, most accurate for forward and back translation, with the authors rating the certainty of evidence as very low to moderate.[25] A 2026 meta-analysis of 30 studies compared patient-specific implants with CAD/CAM splints and found smaller translational deviations with implants and no difference in complication rates.[25]

Orthodontic treatment, often with braces, normally precedes surgery for up to about a year so that the teeth sit in a position that allows the jaws to meet correctly afterwards; Wikipedia notes newer approaches such as surgery-first and clear aligners.[1] Looksmaxxing threads on braces before bimax, braces versus bimax, multi-segment techniques and bimax with maxillary skeletal expansion (MSE) reflect these orthodontic and variant choices.[5][7] Wikipedia also describes rapid palatal expansion osteotomy, in which the maxilla is separated and widened over up to eight weeks with an orthodontic expander.[1]

Orthognathic surgery may be considered to improve facial aesthetics and self-esteem as well as function, and because it usually produces a noticeable change in appearance, a psychological assessment is sometimes part of the process.[1] Moving both jaws changes the skeletal frame that the soft tissue of the lower face rests on, so the projection of the chin, the length of the lower face, the angle of the jaw and the support of the lips and nose can change together.[1] Studies of soft-tissue effects include research on nasolabial changes after double jaw surgery, since moving the maxilla can alter the nose and upper lip.[11]

The 2022 European Journal of Orthodontics meta-analysis reported that orthodontic treatment improved facial attractiveness ratings by about 9 percent versus untreated controls, and that combining orthodontics with orthognathic surgery added about 5.5 percent over orthodontics alone, in studies that were mostly non-randomised with unclear or high risk of bias.[23]

Orthognathic surgery is performed to correct dentofacial deformities, bite problems, jaw asymmetry and obstructive sleep apnea; Wikipedia estimates that nearly 5 percent of the UK or US population has dentofacial deformities that might need it.[1] For obstructive sleep apnea, a related two-jaw procedure called maxillomandibular advancement moves both jaws forward, and Wikipedia says it is one of the most effective surgical treatments for sleep apnea, following jaw advancement observed to relieve sleepiness in three patients in the late 1970s.[21] A 2025 meta-analysis compared outcomes across dentofacial classes and reported the largest percentage reduction in the apnoea-hypopnoea index in class I patients,[9] and a 2026 retrospective cohort of 26 patients with moderate to severe apnea reported an average fall in the apnoea-hypopnoea index of 85.6 percent after advancement planned with a soft-tissue reference line.[25]
A 2008 systematic review analysed 15 studies on the stability of skeletal Class III (underbite) corrections after double-jaw surgery.[10]

According to Wikipedia, initial healing takes 2 to 6 weeks, with bone union and remodelling continuing for a further 2 to 4 months. The jaws are sometimes held together for 1 to 4 weeks, patients usually follow a liquid then soft diet, weight loss is common, and swelling typically fades within weeks although some can last for months.[1] Return to work is possible roughly 2 to 6 weeks after surgery, with recovery rules followed for about 8 weeks.[1]

A systematic review and meta-analysis in the European Journal of Orthodontics examined how patient characteristics, procedure type and country development level relate to quality-of-life scores after orthognathic surgery.[8] Randomised trials in double-jaw patients also address perioperative care such as pain control and nerve blocks.[16][17]

According to Wikipedia, complications include bleeding, swelling, infection (up to 7 percent in cited figures) and numbness from inferior alveolar nerve injury, which usually recovers within about three months but is rarely permanent.[1] A 2026 meta-analysis of 18 bimaxillary studies (1,734 patients) reported neurosensory disturbance in 44.91 percent of bimaxillary cases, 55.18 percent in single-jaw procedures and 40.44 percent after maxillomandibular advancement for sleep apnea, and an infection rate of 3.55 percent after bimaxillary surgery versus 16.34 percent after advancement surgery.[24] The same analysis reported that postoperative obstructive sleep apnea developed in 12.25 percent of bimaxillary cases.[24]

A looksmax.org thread on complications of bimax and trimax surgery and a T Nation forum post in which a member describes a failed double jaw surgery with lasting bone loss show that adverse outcomes are also discussed in these communities.[12][13]

One of the first published jaw-surgery cases was by Simon Hullihen in 1849, and osteotomies of the mandible and maxilla came into use in the 1940s.[1] Hugo Obwegeser (1920 to 2017) trained under Richard Trauner in Graz, worked with Harold Gillies in 1951 to 1952, learned midface advancement from Paul Tessier and presented his techniques to North American surgeons in 1966 at Walter Reed Military Hospital.[19] Wikipedia credits him with the modern Le Fort I and the BSSO and with a paper describing simultaneous operation on both jaws.[19][1] By 1985 jaw osteotomies were also being applied to more extreme deformities and TMJ pain, and in 2002 Raffaini reported the operation under local anaesthesia with sedation to shorten hospital stays.[1]

On looksmax.org, threads ask about cost and recovery, with one poster saying they had heard many people ascend through double jaw surgery and that it is fairly safe, and a reply that price depends on the surgeon.[3] Members in other countries ask whether insurance can cover it for an underbite after seeing social-media accounts of insured patients, and another thread discusses having it done in Poland.[2][4]

Other threads compare bimax with implants, with braces and with multi-segment or MSE variants, and one is titled as arguing that bimax is overrated and overhyped for most people, while others plan it alongside rhinoplasty.[4][5][6][7][14] A T Nation member reported that online peers tell anyone who does not look like a model to get double jaw surgery.[15] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article describes jaw surgery as part of hardmaxxing, the more extreme subset of the culture that also covers off-label substances and skin whitening.[18]

Controlled research on orthognathic surgery covers quality of life,[8] skeletal stability after double-jaw surgery in Class III malocclusion,[10] sleep-apnea outcomes after maxillomandibular advancement,[9][24] soft-tissue changes in the nasolabial area[11] and planning accuracy.[25] The attractiveness meta-analysis of 2022 included orthognathic patients and found a small added rating improvement.[23] Several randomised trials address perioperative care in double-jaw patients, such as pain control and nerve blocks.[16][17] No study has tested the looksmaxxing use of bimax specifically for attractiveness in people without a bite or skeletal problem.

lore.intro: Bimax is among the most discussed hardmaxx procedures on looksmax.org, where members compare surgeons, countries, costs and alternatives.[2][3][4] Wikipedia describes jaw surgery as frequently proposed and discussed among looksmaxxers.[18]

claims.claim: Double jaw surgery makes people "ascend" and is decently safe.
claims.believers: A poster says many people ascend through it and that it is reasonably safe [3].
claims.experts: Reviews report functional and aesthetic benefit and quality-of-life gains, alongside documented risks including infection, bleeding and nerve numbness [1][8].

claims.claim: Bimax can be obtained cheaply or free through insurance for an underbite.
claims.believers: A poster cites a social-media account of an insured patient with an underbite and asks how to do the same [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes surgery as treatment for dentofacial deformity and malocclusion; coverage rules vary by insurer and country and are not described there [1].

claims.claim: Bimax is overrated and overhyped for most people.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues that most people would not gain much from the operation [14].
claims.experts: Studies examine functional and quality-of-life outcomes rather than attractiveness gains for people without a bite or skeletal problem [8].

claims.claim: Implants or braces may achieve similar looks with less surgery.
claims.believers: Threads compare bimax with implants and with braces as alternatives [5][6].
claims.experts: Orthodontics alone does not move the skeletal jaws, whereas orthognathic surgery repositions them [1].

claims.claim: Bimax changes the face more than any non-surgical option.
claims.believers: Threads treat it as the most comprehensive jaw change and compare it with implants and fillers.[4][6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says orthognathic surgery repositions the skeletal jaws and that it changes appearance noticeably; the 2022 meta-analysis reported about 5.5 percent added attractiveness rating over orthodontics alone.[1][23]

claims.claim: Surgery is reliably planned, so the result matches the preview.
claims.believers: Members plan around predicted outcomes and surgeon choice.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes planning software predicts the post-operative shape, and a 2026 preprint found plan-to-outcome discrepancies within 2 mm and 2 degrees with very low to moderate certainty.[1][25]

claims.claim: Nerve numbness and infection are rare enough to ignore.
claims.believers: One poster calls the surgery fairly safe.[3]
claims.experts: A 2026 meta-analysis reported neurosensory disturbance in about 45 percent of bimaxillary cases and infection in about 3.6 percent.[24]

card.summary: Forum shorthand for surgery that repositions both the upper and lower jaw at once; an established orthognathic procedure with documented functional benefits and real surgical risks.
card.aka: Bimaxillary surgery, double jaw surgery, bimax, Le Fort I plus BSSO
card.note: Evidence is for bite and airway outcomes; recovery involves weeks of restrictions, and nerve numbness and infection are documented risks.

quick.overview:
Bimax, or double jaw surgery, means operating on both jaws in one procedure, typically a Le Fort I osteotomy of the upper jaw and a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the lower jaw. It is used for dentofacial deformities, bite problems, airway obstruction and facial disproportion.

Looksmaxxing communities treat it as a major hardmaxx option for changing facial structure. Surgeons usually combine it with orthodontic treatment before and after the operation.
quick.mechanism: The upper and lower jaw bones are cut and moved into new positions, then held with plates and screws while they heal. Wikipedia says infection rates up to 7% are reported and that nerve numbness is usually temporary.
quick.risks: Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness from nerve injury, which usually recovers within about three months but is rarely permanent. Full bone healing takes months, and diet is liquid for a time. Surgery is performed by oral and maxillofacial or plastic surgeons.
